div.head: A p-curve analysis of the emotional Stroop effect among women with eating disorders
div.p: There is evidence that people with eating disorders have an attentional bias to stimuli related to their disorder (Stojek et al., 2018; for a meta-review, see Stott et al., 2021).

Attentional biases have been measured in different ways in the eating disorders literature, such as with the visual probe task testing attention engagement, the reaction time of the spatial cueing task, the reaction time of identifying words in the visual search paradigm, and the reaction time of the emotional Stroop task. Of the different approaches used to assess attentional bias, the emotional Stroop task is the most frequently used tool in prior research to measure attentional biases among people with eating disorders or with elevated eating disorder symptoms (Stott et al., 2021).

Using the emotional Stroop task, an attentional bias is observed when people take longer to identify the ink colour of disorder-related words (e.g., thin, fat, buff) relative to neutral words (e.g., drill, tool). The attentional bias effect based on the emotional Stroop task has been observed in many conceptual replications comparing women with eating disorders to healthy controls over the past thirty years and is a seemingly robust psychological phenomenon (for reviews, see Brooks et al., 2011;Johansson et al., 2005;Stojek et al., 2018). The observed differences between eating disorder and control groups are used to make inferences about the core psychopathology in eating disorders.

Critically, in a recent meta-review, concerns were raised that the results from attentional bias research in eating disorders may be biased and unreliable because the primary-level studies seem to have low statistical power (Stott et al., 2021). This was particularly the case in the literature that used the emotional Stroop task to examine attentional biases among people with eating disorders (Stott et al., 2021;Eynde et al., 2021).
To-date, prior empirical reviews (Brooks et al., 2011;Lavignio et al., 2016) have only assessed the robustness of the literature using meta-analysis and tests of publication bias.

Critically, no prior reviews have quantified the extent of selective reporting in the published literature with statistically significant results and whether the published literature provides evidence of a true underlying effect. The current research addressed this gap in knowledge using a p-curve analysis.

div.head: P-curve Analysis
div.p: There has been growing concern about the rigor and reliability of psychological research in general that stems from many failed replication attempts (Open Science Collaboration, 2015). The failed replications had led some to believe that the psychological literature has low statistical power and that many published findings are false positives (Simmons et al., 2011). Although there are many contributing factors that can help explain failed replications, selective reporting (e.g., manipulated or forced effects) is one agreed upon explanation by may psychology researchers (Baker, 2016). To address the growing concerns about the selective reporting of psychological research, Simonsohn et al. (2014) developed the p-curve analysis to help review published reports with statistically significant results.

A p-curve analysis is used to empirically examine the evidential value of an existing body of research that reports statistically significant results. Evidential value of a statistically significant effect refers to statistically significant findings that are not due solely to selective reporting (Simonsohn et al., 2014). A p-curve analysis plots statistically significant p-values from a literature onto a curve from .01 to .05 to examine the distribution of the p-values. In the p-curve analysis, if an effect is strong and reliable across studies, then the distribution of the p-values testing the effect should pool around the lowest end of the p-distribution (p ≤ .01) creating a right-skewed curve, which is indicative of evidential value. In contrast, if there is no effect, then the p-curve would be flat, as every p-value at or below .05 has a uniform chance of being observed. Likewise, if most p-values pool around the cusp of statistical significance (e.g., .04 and .05) creating a left-skewed curve, then the studies lack evidential value, which suggests the presence of selective reporting in the literature. In this way, the pcurve is a powerful tool that can be used to examine whether the published reports with statistically significant results in an existing body of research provides evidence of a true underlying effect.

Of note, p-curve analyses have been previously used, in conjunction with metaanalysis, in other eating disorder research, such as the efficiency of different prevention tools for reducing eating disorders in university students (Harrer et al., 2019) and cognitive training to change food-related biases (Navas et al., 2021). Also, Carbine and Larson (2019) examined a p-curve for the effect of food-related inhibitory control training. They observed a u-shaped p-curve, which suggests that the literature may have evidential value (many pvalues between .025 and .01), but also that there seems to be some selective reporting in the literature (many p-values between .025 and .05). Carbine and Larson (2019) also showed that the evidential value was weak because it was dependent on the inclusion of a single low pvalue in the analysis. They concluded that the observed effect sizes in the literature were likely biased (inflated) and estimated from low-powered research. In order to improve the reliability of the literature, Carbine and Larson (2019) suggested that researchers should a) pre-register future studies and state an a priori hypothesis, b) be more transparent with reporting methods and results, and report on all collected data, c) conduct a priori power analyses and d) collaborate across laboratories, when possible, to increase sample size. These examples show the benefit of using p-curve analysis for determining the evidential value of a literature, and how results of the p-curve analysis can be used to guide future research.

div.head: The Present Research
div.p: Herein, we examined the evidential value of research that used the emotional Stroop task to assess attentional biases among women with eating disorders. More specifically, we conducted a p-curve analysis of the emotional Stroop research that examined attentional biases among with a diagnosed eating disorder or with eating disorder symptoms. Although any results from the p-curve analysis will be informative, we hypothesized that the p-curve would indicate a lack of evidential value. The reason is that prior reviews have highlighted the low-quality of eating disorders research that used the emotional Stroop task (e.g., Stott et al., 2021). The current research was pre-registered (plus an amendment) before any data collection or analyses were performed and is available on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/9gmr7/?view_only=e87a6a65c32147828eb5e3b4f78876b5).

div.head: Method Inclusion and exclusion criteria
div.p: To be included, reports must have used the emotional Stroop task to test individual differences in reaction times between a sample of healthy individuals (i.e., a control group) and a sample with elevated levels of disordered eating psychopathology or a diagnosed eating disorder. In terms of the emotional Stroop task, reports must have used target words or word/image combinations that were related to body image, food, or general threat (e.g., autonomy threat, ego-self threat, ego-others threat). In addition, to be included, reports should have a clearly stated hypothesis (e.g., "people with elevated eating disorder psychopathology have a slower reaction time than healthy controls on disorder salient stimuli") so as to include the relevant p-value in the p-curve analyses (see Simonsohn et al., 2014). When examining this criterion, we identified nine reports with ambiguous hypotheses. As such, a decision was made post-hoc to include these nine reports if their literature review and introduction indicated they were testing the hypothesis of interest. As well, reports must have reported sufficient inferential statistics (e.g., the df and test statistic of interest) to be included. We also included reports for which enough information was available to infer the df for the p-value re-calculation on the p-curve application. Moreover, reports needed to be independent of other included reports. Reports not meeting any of these inclusion criteria were excluded.

div.head: Selection of Reports
div.p: Two database search strategies were conducted to identify primary-level research reports for inclusion into the p-curve analyses based on the inclusion criteria. The first database search was conducted to locate systematic reviews and meta-analyses of the literature using PubMed, PsycINFO, and ProQuest databases. We identified search terms related to the emotional Stroop task, eating disorders, and reviews to search the title and abstract of records in each database. The Boolean phrase for each database is provided in Table 1. Results were then filtered for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The search was conducted on December 21, 2021, and we located 11 reviews. From these located reviews, primary research reports were extracted that fit the inclusion criteria.

The second database search was conducted to locate primary research reports. Like the first search strategy, the reports had to be on the emotional Stroop task among women with eating disorders or elevated eating disorder psychopathology. We also used the same three databases. The second search was conducted on December 21, 2021.

[Include Table 1] The results of the two searches strategies are reported in Table 2. The pooled sample of research reports that met the inclusion criteria was 50. Of the 50 reports, 32 were included in the p-curve (i.e., p = < .05 on the hypothesis test of interest). The remaining 18 reports had a p-value greater than .05 and so they were not included in the p-curve analyses.

div.head: Data Extraction
div.p: All included reports and their key information (e.g., demographics, extracted test statistic) are reported in Table 2. In line with recommendations for p-curve analyses (Simonsohn et al., 2014), the following information was extracted from each report and included in the extended disclosure tables on OSF (see "Included Studies Extended Disclosure Table " for the extended disclosure table of all included articles and see "P-curve Full Disclosure Table (All Studies)" for all reports screened, including excluded reports and rationale for exclusion): 1) quoted text of the predicted hypothesis; 2) study design; 3) the number of participants and simple demographics (e.g., gender, age, how eating disorder psychopathology was measured); and 4) quoted text with test statistics. In addition, we collected information on how the emotional Stroop task was designed (e.g., type of target and control words, whether images were included) as well as how interference was measured. In cases where a combination of multiple different target words (e.g., body shape/weight and food words) were examined separately, the first p-value of interest to appear in the paper was extracted. In these cases, a secondary robustness test was conducted based on the second pvalue testing the main hypothesis for that category. However, only 18 reports met the criteria for a robustness test, of which seven did not reach statistical significance. Because only 11 reports were included in the robustness p-curve, it is difficult to reliably interpret these results, so they were not reported.

Most reports provided the necessary information for the p-curve shiny app to calculate the exact p-value. When information was missing from a given report, we contacted the author(s) of these reports to provide us with needed information. This was the case for three reports. Unfortunately, none of the authors responded and so these reports were excluded from the analyses. There were also three reports with findings that were not statistically significant and that did not report inferential statistics. These three reports were still included in the disclosure table and considered in interpretations of findings in the Discussion section despite not being included in the p-curve analysis. Hence, the number of reports included in Figure 1 is 47, but 50 reports were considered in the current review.

div.head: Data Analytic Procedure
div.p: All extracted p-values (n= 47, as three non-significant tests were not reported and could not be calculated) were analyzed using the online p-curve app (see: http://www.p- curve.com/app4/). The p-curve app runs two analyses to determine evidential value. The first analysis is a binomial test for both right skew (i.e., testing if most reports fall at the lower end of the curve, such a p < .01, indicating evidential value) and flatter than the 33% power curve (i.e., testing if the p-curve is flatter than one would expect if the reports had 33% power; if this test is significant, it suggests lack of evidential value). The binomial test compares the number of p-values in the lower bin, defined as values below p = .025, to the p-values in the upper bin, defined as values above p = .025 (Simonsohn et al., 2014).

The second analysis is a full continuous test that examines the whole curve rather than binning the results. It includes all p-values and creates z-scores of each score's probability of having its observed value between 0 and .05, if the null hypothesis was true (Simonsohn et al., 2015). To aggregate these values, the p-curve app divides the sum of the z-scores by the square root of the number of tests included in the analysis.

Additionally, a robustness test is run to examine how the curve (both the skewness and 33% power) is affected by removing the lowest or the highest p-values, which allows for identifying extreme values affecting the p-curve (Simonsohn et al., 2015). One can be more confident in sets of reports wherein evidential value is maintained after eliminating the most extreme results.

Lastly, the p-curve app generates a diagnostic plot for the power estimate of included reports. The estimated power and diagnostic plot are created by calculating the Stouffer zscores at each power level between 5% to 90%. The estimated power across reports will be the point with the best fit (i.e., smallest z-score for the Stouffer test).

div.head: Descriptive analyses
div.p: The 50 research reports included 3,996 participants (M = 80, SD = 50.55), with a minimum of 12 participants and a maximum of 321 participants. Fourteen reports provided the ethnicity of their participants. All demographic information associated with each study is reported in Table 2. Of the 50 included research reports, only 14 reported sample demographic information. In these 14 reports, all involved participants that were Caucasian, but the number of Caucasian participants varied across the 14 research reports (range: 52-100%). Furthermore, of the 14 reports, seven recruited Asian participants. Asian participants in these reports ranged between 0.7 -29%. Similarly, six of the 14 reports included African American or Black participants. The number of African American or Black participants in these reports ranged from 1-34%. Likewise, five of the 14 reports included participants that did not identify with provided racial categories (range: 2-22%). Moreover, four of the 14 reports included Latinx participants (range: 1 -17%). Lastly, of the 14 reports two included few participants that were Native American (range: 1.8-3.3%) and two reports included some participants that indicated more than one race or ethnicity (range: 6.5-9%).

As for participants' sex, all 50 reports included female participants. The range of female participants ranged from 55 -100%. However, only six of the 50 reviewed reports included male participants. Among these six reports, male participants in the samples ranged from 14 -45%.

Only five reports included information on socioeconomic status of participants, and each of these reports measured socioeconomic status using different tools. Among these five reports, socioeconomic status was described as "wide" (Ben-Tovim & Walker, 1991), "middle" (Green et al., 1999), and among "the highest three SES classes" (Wilson, 1999).

One more specific study reported the majority (i.e., 56%) of participants made < $20, 000 annually, 8.3% made $20,000 -$50,000 annually, 18.3% made $50,000 -$100,000 annually, and 6.7% made > $100.000 annually among a pool of undergraduates (Lokken, 2001). In two reports, most participants had at least university-entrance levels of education (Preuss et al., 2019;Redgrave et al., 2008). Of the fifty reviewed reports, thirty-two used university students (e.g., undergraduate, medical) as the control group or entire participant pool.

div.head: P-Curve Analysis
div.p: Figure 2 depicts the visual of the p-curve analysis (see the solid line for observed pcurve results). See Table 2 for information on each study. Of the 32 statistically significant reports included in the p-curve analysis, 24 p-values testing the key hypothesis were smaller than .025.

To first examine the right-skewness of the p-curve, results for the binomial test, p = .004, the full continuous test, z = -5.67, p < .0001, and the half continuous test, z = -4.65, p < .0001, were all statistically significant (see Figure 2). The p-curve was also not significantly flatter than the 33% power curve (the dashed curve in Figure 2), binomial: p = .774; half: z = 6.85, p > .999; full: z = 1.81, p = .965. Together, these results indicate evidential value in the literature (i.e., a right-skewed distribution).

[Insert Figure 2 p-curve] Importantly, however, the estimated power across the reports with statistically significant findings was 57%, 90% Confidence Interval = [36%, 75%], as identified by the diagnostic plot in Figure 3. If the same reports were all run again at 57% power, half of the time, the p-curve would be flatter than 33% power curve (see dashed line in Figure 2) and the other half of the time it would be right-skewed.

div.p: We tested the robustness of the findings when excluding the most extreme p-values for both the test of right skewness and the flatter than 33% power curve test. Critically, the full p-curve for right skewness loses evidential value after removing the seven lowest p-values (i.e., close to a quarter of the included reports; see Figure 4a). Likewise, the half pcurve for right skewness loses evidential value after removing just three of the lowest pvalues (Figure 4b). Thus, excluding a few of the lowest p-values eliminates evidential value.

In contrast, the full p-curve was not statistically flatter from the 33% power curve even after removing upwards of 15 reports with the lowest p-values (see Figure 4c), which suggests the presence of evidential value.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: We conducted a review of 50 emotional Stroop reports among women with eating disorders symptoms or a diagnosed eating disorder. Of the 50 reports, 47 were able to be included in the p-curve analyses to examine the evidential value of the literature. Based on Stott and colleagues' (2021) meta-review of the attentional bias literature in eating disorders, we hypothesized that the p-curve would be indicative of no evidential value (i.e., flat).
Unexpectedly, the p-curve had a significantly right-skewed distribution, which indicates evidential value (Simonsohn et al., 2015).

Critically, however, other results from the p-curve analyses suggests that evidential value was weak as the robustness test indicated that the evidential value was dependent on the inclusion of a few low p-values. In particular, the full p-curve loses evidential value after removing seven of the lowest p-values. Likewise, the half p-curve loses evidential value after removing only three of the lowest p-values. Taken together, the results of the p-curve analyses indicate that results from the literature examining attentional biases among women with eating disorders using the emotional Stroop task should be interpreted with considerable caution.

Of import, the estimated power across studies with statistically significant results in the p-curve analysis was below 80%-the minimally acceptable level of power in psychological research. In addition, even though the p-curve was quantitatively different from the 33% power curve (see the dashed line in Figure 2), the visual shape of the p-curve resembled the shape of a 33% power curve. Specifically, the p-curve, depicted in Figure 2 as the solid line, has an increased number of p-values at the .01, .03, and .05 levels. The pvalues at .02 and .04 fall below the dashed power line. The p-curve begins to appear flatter than the 33% curve after removing the six lowest p-values, where the 33% power analysis becomes approximately p = .10. These findings indicate that many of the included reports likely have less than 33% power, which is woefully below the traditional minimum of 80% power used in psychology research.

It is well-established that results from low-power research are unreliable because they have a low chance of detecting a true effect (Cohen & Rogers, 2003). They may also not reflect a true effect (e.g., Button et al., 2013). For these reasons, results from low-power research are almost always inconclusive and so should be interpreted with considerable caution. As such, although there is evidential value based on the p-curve analysis in the current research, many of the analyzed reports have low power, which undermines confidence in the results of the literature examining attentional biases among women with eating disorders using the emotional Stroop task.

Another concern with the reports included in the p-curve analysis is that some did not have a clear hypothesis. Simonsohn et al. (2015) advised that only p-values directly relevant to the stated hypothesis should be included in the p-curve analysis. The reason is that the accuracy and reliability of the null-hypothesis significance test rely on clear, theory-driven, a priori hypotheses. Critically, when extracting information from the included reports in the pcurve analyses, nine reports did not clearly state a theory-driven hypothesis (reports that found a statistically significant effect: Ben-Tovim et al., 1989;Channon et al., 1988;Cooper & Fairburn, 1993;Davidson & Wright, 2002;Green et al., 1994;Kanakam et al., 2013; reports that did not find a statistically significant effect: Preuss et al., 2019;Tapper et al., 2008;Tressler, 2008). That said, we made the decision post-hoc to include these nine reports to ensure that we included as much as possible of the relevant literature in the p-curve analyses. Of note, in an exploratory analysis, the results remained virtually the same after excluding these nine reports (see OSF for these analyses).
We are also concerned with reports on attentional biases among women with eating disorders using the emotional Stroop task that were not included in the p-curve analyses.

More specifically, there were 18 reports that had a p-value greater than .05 (Green & Rogers, 1993;Hodge et al., 2020;Jansen et al., 1998;Kuehfuss, 2007;Lattimore et al., 2000;Lee et al., 2017;Markis, 2015;McManus et al., 1996;Ogden & Greville, 1993;Perpiñá et al., 1998;Preuss et al., 2019;Prystanski, 2011;Quinton, 1998;Scholar, 1999;Seddon & Waller, 2000;Tapper et al., 2008;Tressler, 2008;Wilson, 1999), which precluded their inclusion in the pcurve analyses. When juxtaposed with the 32 reports included in the p-curve analysis, the fact that there are at least 18 reports (36% of the reports that fit our inclusion criteria) with results that are not statistically significant is indicative of contradictions in the published literature.

Critically, the contradictions in the literature may be due, in part, to low power (Maxwell, 2004). Unfortunately, the p-curve application does not consider the non-significant results when generating the power estimate, so we do not know if the results from reports that are not statistically significant are adequately powered or not. As such, the results indicating evidential value from the p-curve analyses should be interpreted considering the substantial number of reports with results that are not statistically significant.
It is possible that methodological differences may exist between reports with statistically significant results and reports with results that were not statistically significant.

For example, Tabri and Palmer (2020) noted word repetition (people are faster at recognizing words they have already seen) and the use of unmatched words on different lexical characteristics (e.g., number of letters, syllables, orthographic neighbourhoods, and frequency of usage in the English language) as limitations in the eating disorders emotional Stroop literature, among others. These differences in the task and nature of the stimuli may help explain differences between reports with and without statistically significant results. For instance, among the statistically significant reports reviewed herein, there was more variance in the type of word, or word and image stimuli compared to reports that found no statistically significant difference between groups. As well, some non-statistically significant reports only used food words and control words or body shape/weight words and control words, compared to the statistically significant reports which more commonly combined the two groups of target words (i.e., had both food and body words). It is possible that these methodological differences may help explain why some reports have statistically significant results and other do not. Future research should examine methodological differences between reports with statistically significant findings and reports with results that are not statistically significant in a more rigorous and systematic approach.

The findings of the current research also have implications for interpreting the results of prior reviews on the emotional Stroop task among women with eating disorders. Of note, we identified 11 meta-analytic reviews (see Figure 1) from which we included many of the reports in the p-curve analyses. Critically, like the included reports, the findings from these reviews should be interpreted with considerable caution. The reason is that the inclusion of low-powered reports in the prior reviews will produce conclusions that are unreliable and inaccurate (e.g., Aguinis et al., 2011).

In sum, the results of the p-curve analyses and the fact that there are many published reports with results that are not statistically significant should give everyone pause about the reliability and accuracy of results based on the emotional Stroop task in the eating disorders literature. Accordingly, there is a need for high-powered (i.e., at least 80%; Bakker et al., 2016) pre-registered research. Often, it is difficult to determine the effect size for a priori power analyses and so researchers can consider initially conducting a hypothesis-generating or exploratory study followed by a high-powered replication study that confirms the results (see more information about sample size justification and a priori power analyses in Lakens, 2022). The research conducted by Tabri and Palmer (2020) using the emotional Stroop task in the context of eating disorders provides an example of this approach with pre-registration.

A possible limitation of the current research is that we only evaluated published research that provided the necessary inferential statistics for the p-curve analysis. As such, there may be unpublished research that could have been included in the p-curve analysis.

However, it is likely that many of these unpublished reports have results that were not statistically significant, which is consistent with the notion of publication bias. Accordingly, the inconsistent findings observed in the reviewed literature should be interpreted with the understanding that there are likely other reports that were not published because they had results that were not statistically significant.

Another limitation has to do with the p-curve analysis approach. Results of a recent simulation study showed that the p-curve analysis overestimates power when there is heterogeneity in effect and sample sizes among the included reports (Brunner & Schimmack, 2020). As such, to the extent there are differences in sample size and effect sizes across the included reports, the 57% power estimated across reports included in the p-curve analysis may be an overestimation. This means that the overall estimated power may be even lower.

Furthermore, from our review, we observed that emotional Stroop research in context of eating disorders may have limited external validity. Most reports involved women with eating disorders and so it is unclear whether findings generalize to populations of men with eating disorders. Likewise, there was a tendency for reports to rely on samples of undergraduate women as both the control group and the group with elevated disordered eating characteristics. With this approach, it is unclear whether findings would generalize to populations who do not have access to post-secondary education. As well, there was limited information on the socioeconomic status of participants in the reports, but the use of university participants suggest middle to upper-class participants in these samples. Moreover, most reports recruited participants residing in "Western" countries (e.g., Canada, USA, and the UK), except for two reports that involved samples from Iran (n = 98) and Korea (n = 39).
Taken together, the external validity of results to men, people without access to postsecondary education, and to people residing in non-Western countries remains unresolved.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Concerns have been raised about the low power of results from research examining attentional biases among women with eating disorders using the emotional Stroop task (e.g., Stott et al., 2021;Van den Eynde et al., 2011). Herein, we used p-curve analyses to empirically determine the evidential value of the literature reporting statistically significant results. Although results suggest the presence of evidential value, a robustness check indicated that the evidential value was dependent on the inclusion of few small p-values.

Moreover, most of the included reports had low power and results from low-powered research are inconclusive. There was also a substantial number of reports with results that were not statistically significant, which precluded their inclusion in the p-curve analyses. This pattern of contradictions in the literature is consistent with the literature being low-powered.
Accordingly, results from research examining attentional biases among women with eating disorders using the emotional Stroop task should be interpreted with considerable caution.

div.head: Public Significance Statement
div.p: Concerns have been raised about the low quality of research examining attentional biases among women with eating disorders using the emotional Stroop task. In the current research, we observed that the evidential value of primary research reporting differences between women with and without eating disorders was equivocal and had low statistical power. These results can guide researchers towards conducting more rigorous research on attentional biases among people with eating disorders.
